title: TB4-08042
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "claimant") claims to be a citizen of Turkey and requests protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 PROCEDURAL ISSUE - unaccompanied minor

The claimant was 17 years-old on the date of the hearing (born XXXX XXXX, 1997). The claimant's uncle, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Canada, was appointed as his designated representative (DR). The DR was present at the hearing. The claimant provided the majority of the oral evidence, but the DR also contributed oral evidence when needed and was not prevented from doing so at other times.
The allegations are set out in the Basis of Claim form (BOC).2 The following is a summary.
The claimant suffered various forms of mistreatment because of his Kurdish ethnicity, his Alevi religion, and his pro-Kurdish political opinions.

For example, he was shunned by his teachers and classmates. In XXXX 2012 his teacher took the claimant to the principal's office for failing to study the Koran and saying he would not need the verses since he was Alevi; he was asked to put out his hands so he could be hit with a stick, but when he refused he was hit on his back. The claimant's father complained the next day and argued with the teacher. The teacher called police and police took the claimant and his father to the police station where they were kicked, punched, and beaten with truncheons. Police let them go warning the father to behave himself. After this, the family began looking for ways to send the claimant out of Turkey.

The claimant then participated in XXXX XXXX demonstrations in his city in XXXX 2013. He was detained along with several others. He was questioned and beaten in detention. They let him go after 15 hours of detention and warned him not to be involved in such things in the future. After this, his family made efforts to obtain a visa so he could leave Turkey, but the application was unsuccessful.

A year later, in XXXX 2014 the claimant was keen on learning Kurdish. Having printed some text from the internet he was reading it while riding a bus. The bus was stopped and two plainclothes police approached the claimant and took away his material. The claimant was brought to the security directorate where he was questioned as to whether the text had anything to do with the PKK, accused him of publicly promoting Kurdish language, and trying to incite Kurdish nationalism. He was beaten and tortured. The claimant was released after 24 hours and authorities again warned his father that he should watch his son to prevent future trouble.

Determined to send him out of Turkey, the claimant's father applied for a study permit for the United States of America (USA). They obtained the visa at the end of XXXX 2014 and the claimant left Turkey on XXXX XXXX, 2014 to the USA. The claimant attended the two-week course in the USA, but his family's intention was to have the claimant go to Canada to join his uncle upon completion of the course. The claimant left Boston and went to XXXX XXXX XXXX in Buffalo where arrangements were made for him to request protection in Canada, and he did on September 2, 2014.
I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. My reasons are as follows. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's oral testimony and documentary evidence establish that, on a balance of probabilities, he is a citizen of Turkey.3 Credibility

When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.4 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.5
Some of the claimant's evidence was not reliable. Mistreatment at school prior to XXXX 2012.

The claimant was vague and evasive in describing any serious mistreatment prior to the alleged incident in XXXX 2012 where his teacher hit him with a stick for not having studied the Koran. The claimant was in grade 12 by this time, but had not alleged any such mistreatment until then, particularly for not having studied religion (the Koran and reciting the verses). The claimant said that his school was comprised mostly of nationalistic extremists and that he had been studying religion since grade five. As such, I wondered why there had not been such incidents before. The claimant explained that there were, but it was more intense in grade 12. However, the claimant could not describe any previous incidents. The claimant said they (the Kurd/Alevi students) were being mistreated and beaten. They were taken to the blackboard and mistreated. This did not happen in religion class, but other classes. This was vague and nondescript as such I took it as non-responsive. Asked for further information, the claimant said the mistreatment was due to their background and when they could not answer questions. This was still vague.

The claimant then said he was beaten when he was in grades 10 and 11 as well, but could not remember how many times, and that his father came to the school each time, but that nothing ever changed. However, this is not contained in the narrative. The claimant explained that problems had accumulated and that it became more intense at that point (in XXXX 2014). I reject this explanation. It is reasonable to expect the claimant to include previous physical beatings that had occurred a number of times, and the fact that his father had attempted to rectify the matter with the school to no avail, rather than simply stating in the narrative that he had been "shunned" by students and teachers. There is a significant difference between the two.

I find the claimant's evidence with respect to the seriousness of the mistreatment prior to XXXX 2012 is not reliable. This is an attempt by the claimant to embellish and exaggerate the seriousness of any mistreatment suffered, and given the context of the question (wondering why there had not been mistreatment prior) casts doubt on whether the XXXX 2012 incident occurred. XXXX 2012 - beating at school

The claimant states in his narrative and repeated at the hearing that he was taken to the principal's office and hit by his religion teacher. She was going to discipline the claimant for not having studied the Koran and saying the verses were not important to him since he would not need them as an Alevi. The claimant refused to hold out his hands and the teacher then used the measuring stick to strike the claimant on his back.

The claimant said he had suffered bruises on his back and his father took him to a doctor for treatment. The claimant could not remember the name of the doctor, the clinic name, or even the name of the street the clinic was on. That seemed strange considering the claimant said it was only a short walk from his home. However, the claimant was only 15 years-old at the time and was relying on his father for assistance, and the claimant knew it was a government clinic that was a short walk from his home.

The claimant did not provide documentary evidence to support the allegation of his beating and visit to the clinic for treatment. The claimant explained that his father tried to get a document from the doctor at the clinic, but the doctor refused to post-date a letter. The claimant's father states in his letter that the doctor told him that the reports are past-dated and did not want to lose his job; that it was illegal to write an old-dated report.6 It would seem then that the claimant's father was asking the doctor to post-date a document which the doctor would not do. However, it is not clear at all, whether the claimant or his father had asked for a copy of any record that might have existed already for the event or even the doctor's confirmation that he did treat the claimant for injuries on a specified date.

The effort to obtain a document that could be obtained with reasonable effort and that it is reasonable to expect would be available is insufficient. Since this was a government hospital it is reasonable to expect they would have a record of any treatment they provided. The claimant and/or his father do not adequately explain why a copy of that record, or a letter from the doctor confirming past treatment (as opposed to post-dating a document) would not be available.

I draw an adverse inference and find the evidence with respect suffering injuries and receiving treatment as a result of the incident in XXXX 2012 is not reliable. At best, the allegation is a fabrication to embellish the nature of harm feared by the claimant. XXXX 2012 - beating by police

After the claimant was beaten by his teacher in XXXX 2012 the claimant's father went to the school and argued with the teacher. The teacher subsequently called police. Police arrived at the claimant's home and took the claimant and his father to the police station. At the station the claimant and his father were separated. The police asked about the reason for discussing with the teacher and said that they were allowed to do what they want. The police said that the Koran was their bible and questioned why the claimant would not memorize it. The police then proceeded to beat the claimant for half an hour by punching, kicking, and hitting the claimant with a truncheon.

The claimant said he had swelling and bruising. His father had similar injuries as he was beaten as well. However, neither the claimant nor his father went for medical treatment. This makes no sense. The claimant was taken to the doctor after being hit by his teacher with a measuring stick because there was bruising on his back, yet after being beaten by police for half an hour with punches, kicks and a truncheon, there was no visit to the doctor. The claimant explained that it was his decision not to go for medical treatment. I reject this explanation. It is entirely unreasonable to believe the injuries caused by being beaten by police to a half hour (with punches, kicks and truncheon) would not have required a visit to the doctor, but that the injuries caused by the school teacher's measuring stick did.

Also, the claimant said at the hearing that he and his father were separated and he did not hear what police said to his father. However, in his narrative the claimant states that the police called his father an infidel. The claimant explained that the police called them infidels before they separated them. I reject this explanation. The claimant's narrative is clear that the name-calling occurred after or during the beating. The claimant states, "My father and I were punched, kicked, and beaten with truncheons. They police called my father an infidel." Also, the claimant said he could not remember whether the police had said anything else. This seems to have been a convenient tool used by the claimant when there were gaps in the testimony that could not be explained.
Based on both the above, I find the evidence with respect to being taken to a police station and being beaten is not reliable.

Furthermore, based on the unreliability of the evidence with respect to being beaten at school and the evidence with respect to being taken to a police station and beaten, I find that on a balance of probabilities, the evidence with respect to the allegations of the events of XXXX 2012 is not reliable. Delay in leaving

The claimant states in his narrative that after the XXXX 2012 incident his father began to consider sending him abroad to be with his uncle in Canada. They applied for his passport which was received in XXXX 2013. However, nothing else was done. Then the claimant states in his narrative that it was after an alleged incident in XXXX 2013 when the claimant was once again beaten by police, that the family made efforts to obtain a visa to Canada so the claimant could leave Turkey. This is six months after the alleged incident in XXXX 2012 after which the family started to look for ways so the claimant could leave Turkey.

The claimant explained that they started planning after the XXXX incident, and it took eight months because he wanted to complete the school year. This is an unreasonable reason to delay leaving. The claimant states he was having problems at school and the family was worried he would not be able to complete his education in Turkey. The family took the step of applying for a passport. While the claimant may not have been in imminent danger, the family believed it was necessary to send him out of the country, so it is reasonable to expect that further efforts would have been made at the time.

The claimant then added that they had in-fact been trying, but that his uncle said it would be difficult to get status in Europe. The DR added that he had been in Germany for many years and he was still deported. The DR added that they did start discussing leaving in XXXX 2012, and told them to get a passport and look for a smuggler to leave Turkey, but this took a lot of time. The DR said the family applied for a Canadian visitor visa in XXXX or XXXX of 2013 but it was rejected. This is still six months after the incidents, and even considering looking for a smuggler, does not explain why applying for a student visa (which does not require the services of smuggler) took so long. Asked why they did not apply in XXXX, the DR said they did, but it was refused.

There was no documentary evidence offered to support the allegation that there were several attempts at obtaining a Canadian visa as early as XXXX 2013. Given the conflicting evidence on this issue, I draw an adverse inference and find the evidence with respect to efforts to leave the country is not reliable.
I draw an adverse inference and find that the necessary subjective fear is lacking and the evidence with respect to the risk of harm is not reliable. XXXX 2013 - XXXX XXXX protests

The claimant states in his narrative and repeated at the hearing that he participated in XXXX XXXX protests in his city. On XXXX XXXX, 2013 police tried to disperse the protests and arrested several people including the claimant. During detention the claimant was questioned about the organization of the protests. The claimant was detained for 15 hours and again punched, kicked, and beaten with truncheons. The claimant was bruised and had a bloody nose. After release the claimant was taken to the doctor by his father.

The claimant did not provide any documentary evidence to support the allegation that he had visited a doctor for treatment of injuries suffered at this time. As with the incident above, the claimant explained that his father tried to get a document, but the doctor refused to past-date a document. For the same reasons as stated above (XXXX 2012 - beating at school), I find this effort to be insufficient given it is reasonable to expect the clinic would likely have records of treatment of patients, especially when medication was issued.
I draw an adverse inference and find the evidence with respect to the XXXX 2013 incident is not reliable.

Furthermore, the claimant said at the hearing that police had dispersed the crowd and police caught him, kicked, and beat him at the protest site. However, in his narrative the claimant only states that he was beaten while in detention. The claimant explained that he did not include the beating at the protest site because he wanted to focus on the main issue. I reject this explanation. The main issue is that the claimant was beaten for participating at a protest. It is reasonable to include all the mistreatment suffered on account of this participation.
I find the evidence with respect to the XXXX 2013 incident is not reliable.

Furthermore, the claimant said that while he was in detention at the security directorate his father tried to get him out, but was denied. However, the claimant does not include this information for this particular incident in his narrative. In his narrative he states that it was in XXXX 2014, a year later, when he was once again taken to the security directorate and held for 24 hours that his father had come to the station, but police would not let him see the claimant.

The claimant explained that he knew his father had come, but he just wanted to mention the detention (not his father's efforts to get him released). I reject this explanation. The claimant certainly believed it was important to mention his father's efforts in an incident that occurred a year later and it is reasonable then to expect he would include other efforts his father made in other incidents. It is more likely the claimant was conflating events.
I find the evidence with respect to the incident of XXXX 2013 is not reliable. XXXX XXXX, 2014 - reading on a bus

The claimant states in his narrative that he wanted to learn to read Kurdish and one day, when he was practicing on a bus, he was approached by two plainclothes police officers who took his reading material and took the claimant to the security directorate. At the security directorate he was detained for 24 hours. His father was called and he came to the station, but was not allowed to see the claimant. During detention the claimant was tortured as police interrogated him about the why he was reading the Kurdish text, whether it had anything to do with the PKK and Kurdish nationalism.

However, at the hearing the claimant said that this occurred in XXXX 2013. The claimant explained that he was confused about the date. I reject this explanation. The claimant was asked to confirm his response and agreed that this incident happened "a year ago." Since the hearing was in XXXX 2014 it is reasonable to expect the claimant to know that this incident only happened a few months ago in the same year, particularly since it was only a few weeks after this that the claimant left Turkey.

Furthermore, the claimant said he did not know whether his father made any effort to come and see him at the security directorate. The claimant explained that he knew his father came to the station, but was not aware of any conversation. I reject this. The claimant stated in his narrative that his father was denied access to the claimant. The question was not about any conversation, but whether his father had come to the station.

After a break in the hearing the claimant further explained that he was nervous as this was the first time he was before a judge. I reject this explanation as well. The claimant did not seem to have problems remembering other less significant information. While I understand claimants may be nervous in such circumstances, and even given that he was a minor, although not by much, this does not adequately explain the inconsistencies.

The claimant makes no mention of medical treatment after this incident nor was there documentary evidence to indicate that he had received medical treatment. The BOC indicates to specify whether claimants have received medical treatment. In this particular incident the claimant alleges he was subjected to torture, "falaka," in addition to punching, kicking, and beating with a truncheon. Falaka is a beating of the soles of the feet. It is highly likely given these circumstances the claimant would have needed medical attention and completely implausible that he would not have sought medical attention after such an ordeal.
Based on all the above, I find the evidence with respect to the event of XXXX 2014 is not reliable. Detentions and beatings in general

When the claimant first requested protection in Canada he stated that he was having problems at school because he is Kurdish. When asked for the reason he was seeking protection the claimant stated simply that, "I am having troubles at school, because I am Kurdish and Alevi the teacher isolates me from lessons. In my school I wasn't feeling safe. The teachers and friends give me a hard time." The claimant said there was nothing else to add. The claimant fails to mention any detentions or beatings.

The claimant explained that the person in Canada questioning was a police officer and he is fearful when he sees police. I reject this explanation. Firstly, the claimant does not even mention that his teacher beat him. Further, the evidence with respect to the mistreatment suffered at the hands of police has been found to be unreliable. Further, the claimant's purpose in coming to Canada was for the very purpose of protection, he had the assistance of XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX), and an uncle in Canada who had been through the refugee process. It is therefore reasonable to expect the claimant would have been prepared for his entry interview. Furthermore, this explanation is not contained in his BOC narrative where the claimant tried to pre-emptively explain the omission of significant events of detention and police brutality.

The claimant explained in his narrative and repeated at the hearing that he was told that he would be able to tell his entire story later. I reject this. While I understand the intake interview is not a substitute for a refugee hearing and its purpose is not to gather the entire details of the claim, this was an open-ended question for the claimant to state his reason for requesting protection. It is reasonable to expect that police brutality and torture while in detention, beating at a protest, and arrests for simply reading text, and even a beating from a teacher would be mentioned before the fact that his teachers "isolate him from lessons."

Finally, the claimant explained that he did not have his uncle with him at the intake interview. While it is not readily apparent that the claimant's uncle was appointed his designated representative at the time of the intake interview, it is clear the officer knew the claimant was a minor as this is part of the basis for finding an exemption under the Safe Third Country Agreement.7 It is also clear that the claimant's uncle was interviewed at the time as well. I also note that while the claimant is a minor, it is just barely. When he arrived in Canada he was just weeks away from his 17th birthday. Given his age, and that he had been studying in the USA for some weeks prior to his arrival, and that he was very able to answer questions on his own during the hearing, I do not consider the absence of his uncle as reason sufficient to explain such significant omissions.
I find the evidence with respect the alleged beatings and detention at the hands of the teacher and police is not reliable. Kurd and Alevi

The claimant alleges he suffers mistreatment because he is Kurd and Alevi, but all the evidence with respect to the alleged mistreatment is unreliable. Based on the above, I may also find that the evidence with respect to the claimant being Kurd and Alevi is also unreliable. Particularly so since the documentary evidence provided is not probative in that the letter from the Canadian XXXX XXXX Centre does not indicate how they determined the claimant is Alevi.8 The letter from the XXXX XXXX Cultural Association is equally uninformative except that the claimant's family participated in the events of the association and the claimant's father is a registered member.9 I may infer that only Alevis would join such a centre, this need not be the case. The letter from the XXXX Kurdish Community is somewhat persuasive that the claimant is Kurdish.10
Despite the unreliable evidence with respect to the allegations of harm, I find, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is Kurd and Alevi. Persecution as Kurd and Alevi - Section 96

The claimant's own evidence of persecution is not reliable and does not establish that he has a well-founded fear of persecution just because he is Kurd and Alevi. The documentary evidence provided by the claimant does not establish that all Kurd and Alevi people have a well-founded fear of persecution (although those who are activists, or involved in PKK activities or others of various profiles might).11 The documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package supports that there might be some Kurd and Alevi who do suffer persecution, but they are typically of a certain profile which the claimant does not possess.12
There is not more than a mere possibility that the claimant suffer persecution on account of his Kurd ethnicity or Alevi religion.
The claimant is not a Convention refugee. Residual elements of a claim - Section 97

The analysis above applies to a section 97 analysis. There is no residual information that could be assessed differently. Since the claimant faces no more than a mere possibility of serious harm, it is not likely he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.
The claimant is not a person in need of protection.

For all of the above reasons, the claimant does not have a well-founded of persecution and would not be subjected personally, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, upon return to return to Turkey.
Accordingly, the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The claim is rejected. (signed) "B. Volpentesta" B.
